prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which enabled incretin-based therapies for diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single prize part, B017, credited to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The case is a continuous chain from gut-hormone physiology (Holst on secretion and action in humans, Drucker on proglucagon processing and receptor biology, Mojsov on the bioactive GLP-1(7-36) peptide) to a drug class with large randomised outcome evidence in glycaemia, weight, cardiovascular and renal disease. It is original, independently confirmed over decades and mature. A physiology-centred citation keeps the award inside physiology or medicine, and it lets us say openly that long-acting analogues followed from the biology without naming a drug-design contribution. I do not think a second part is needed. Nothing in the first round shows a second achievement whose credit I can defend within the three-person limit, and adding one would trade a clean, near-unanimous first part for a contested second.
statement.case_against: Credit remains the weak point. The Mojsov versus Habener priority question is not settled by the supplied evidence, and it should be treated as an unresolved risk and not as a closed matter. Omitting Knudsen leaves out the designer of liraglutide and semaglutide, which delivered most of the clinical impact, so the award can be read as incomplete. The citation wording limits that gap but does not remove it. A single part also leaves out strong clinical achievements (CAR-T, BCR-ABL inhibition, anti-TNF), and I accept that cost because none of them has a clean credit set on the supplied names.

responses.point: Calls the Mojsov versus Knudsen choice for the third seat a close call, since his opening ballot made the opposite trade-off, and asks whether a physiology-centred citation can acknowledge the analogue drugs without making Knudsen necessary.
responses.response: I had the same trio as you at opening and moved for the same reason, so I take the doubt seriously. Even so, my answer is that the third seat is a question of what the prize identifies. Mojsov's work on the active peptide is part of the discovery that made a drug conceivable, whereas Knudsen's analogue design is the next step, a major one but an engineering and development step. I would not name Knudsen. I would make the principle explicit in the citation by saying the discoveries 'enabled incretin-based therapies'. That wording concedes the gap openly. It does not pretend the drugs arose by themselves.

responses.point: As chair, says the unanimous support does not prove merit, lists the risk that the prize rewards commercial scale as much as originality, and asks whether a second part (B024 or B006) would strengthen the award or dilute a near-unanimous first choice.
responses.response: I agree that commercial scale should not stand in for originality, and that is another reason to keep the citation on physiology. On a second part, I considered B024 and B006 again. For B024, Rowley's upstream BCR-ABL work is outside the names and the contribution is largely drug development on earlier recognised biology. For B006, Eshhar is missing and Rosenberg's role is a separate adoptive-transfer lineage. Neither gives a clean trio, so a second part would add an attribution dispute and weaken the first part. I therefore prefer B017 alone.

responses.point: Accepts the gap from leaving out Knudsen but says it should be stated openly, and suggests CAR-T may do better as a single-achievement prize if B017 is unsettled.
responses.response: I agree that the gap should be stated and not hidden. That is why I have kept 'enabled incretin-based therapies' in the citation. On CAR-T as a stand-alone option I partly agree, since June and Sadelain make a cleaner pair than the trio. But B017 is not unsettled. All six of us now hold the same trio and the same weakness, so I see no reason to put it aside for B006. I keep B006 as my first alternative if the committee found the GLP-1 credit unworkable.

responses.point: Cites central appetite effects as part of the GLP-1 physiology case, and frames the citation around the hormone and its active peptide form.
responses.response: I agree on framing the citation around the hormone and its active form. I would give central appetite effects less weight in the citation. The chair's file notes that the CNS mechanism is still being worked out, and the discovery case is already complete from gut-pancreas physiology and the active peptide. Mentioning obesity as a therapeutic indication is enough, and it avoids tying the credited names to an unfinished mechanism.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1 peptide can be defended against Habener and other early investigators, which I cannot verify from the supplied evidence.
Whether colleagues will accept a physiology-centred citation that leaves out Knudsen, or will see the omission as too large to leave.
Whether a second part would be worthwhile if a clean credit set emerges for B006 (for example June and Sadelain alone) or B018.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My field is autoimmunity and rheumatology, which is topically close to B018 (anti-TNF, an alternative) and to CAR-T in autoimmune disease. My profile documents no collaboration with any credited candidate on the shortlist, and I request no recusal.
